abstract: Imprinted genes regulate development and metabolism and are implicated in both rare developmental syndromes and common diseases. Genomic imprinting is conventionally inferred from parent-of-origin effects (POEs), identified as differences between heterozygotes who inherited an allele from their mother and those who inherited it from their father. However, such differences can also be caused by indirect parental genetic effects, i.e. the fact that the genotype of a parent can be associated with behavioral or environmental changes that affect the phenotype of their offspring. No study of the human methylome has so far accounted for this confounding effect when inferring imprinted loci. Here, we jointly estimate direct, maternal, paternal and parent-of-origin effects at 850,055 methylation probes from whole blood in 2,438 parent-offspring trios from Generation Scotland. Of 5,435 probes with apparent POE signal, 4,974 (91.5%) fall below threshold once parental genotypes are included, suggesting that the vast majority are not attributable to imprinting alone. We treat the 281 remaining probes, 17 on the X chromosome and 42 not previously reported, as a conservative, high-confidence set, map them to 1,118 SNP loci linked to gene expression and protein abundance, and identify 27 probes where imprinting and indirect parental genetic effects both contribute. In a hold-out set of relatives, 250 of the 281 show familial resemblance consistent with a combination of imprinting and parental effects. Our results highlight the importance of accounting for indirect parental genetic effects when interpreting putative imprinting regions.
